captions: Let's break down the Molbio Diagnostics I-P-O —
a nine hundred and forty crore issue from a company with a genuinely unique product,
and an unusual twist when it comes to valuation.
We'll cover what it does, its financials,
where the money goes, why it has no listed peer,
and how much you'd need to apply.
This is education, not investment advice.
So what does Molbio do?
It makes a device called Truenat — a portable,
lab-grade molecular testing machine that can diagnose disease in about an hour,
right at the point of care, even in a remote village clinic.
It's best known for tuberculosis testing,
but it runs dozens of other infectious and non-communicable disease tests too.
It's a made-in-India platform used around the world.
And it has a smart model — it sells the machines,
and then the recurring test cartridges that go with them.
Razor and blade — a recurring-revenue tail.
Let's go deeper.
Who uses Molbio's Truenat?
Its anchor customers are governments and public-health programs —
the platform is I-C-M-R validated and built into India's National T-B Elimination Programme.
It's also one of only two rapid molecular T-B platforms endorsed by the World Health Organization,
patented in more than a hundred countries and used well beyond India.
On order book — a device maker doesn't have one.
Instead it earns recurring revenue from test cartridges across a large installed base of machines,
for T-B, H-I-V, dengue, hepatitis and more.
That razor-and-blade tail is the real prize.
The financials are strong.
Revenue for FY twenty twenty-six was about one thousand four hundred and forty-six crore,
up nearly forty-two percent.
Net profit was around one hundred and sixty-seven crore,
up fifteen percent.
So this is a genuinely profitable, fast-growing business —
the profit grew slower than revenue because it's investing in research and capacity.
The grey market premium is near twenty-two percent,
but as always, that's unofficial.
Now — where does your money go?
And here's the catch.
Of the nine hundred and forty crore issue,
only two hundred crore — about twenty-one percent —
is a fresh issue that goes into the company.
The other seven hundred and forty crore,
nearly eighty percent, is an Offer for Sale —
existing investors selling their stakes and cashing out.
So when you apply,
most of your money is buying out people who are exiting,
not funding the company's growth.
That small fresh-issue slice — the two hundred crore —
what does it fund?
About a hundred and five crore builds an R and D facility and a centre of excellence through its subsidiary Bigtec,
plus office space.
Another seventy-two crore buys plant and machinery for its factories in Goa and Visakhapatnam.
The rest is general corporate purposes.
So the fresh money is well spent on research and capacity —
there just isn't very much of it,
because most of the issue is a sell-down.
Now — the competitors, and here Molbio is unusual.
Its own offer document says it has NO listed peer to compare with.
There simply isn't another company like it on the exchange.
People often name Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis or Thyrocare —
but those are lab-SERVICE chains that run tests; Molbio MAKES the testing devices.
Different business, not a real peer.
The catch: with no peer,
there's no P-E yardstick to tell you whether it's cheap or expensive.
So judge it on its growth — revenue up over forty percent —
and its margins,
and be a little wary of a price that no rival is keeping honest.
Should you subscribe?
The strengths are real — it's a unique,
made-in-India platform used globally,
it's fast-growing and profitable,
and it has a lovely recurring stream from test kits.
The watch-outs —
nearly eighty percent of the issue is investors cashing out,
there's no listed peer so it's hard to value,
and it's priced richly with no benchmark to check it against.
The takeaway — a genuinely impressive company,
but mostly a sell-down at a price no peer anchors.
Size any bet with that in mind.
How do you apply, and how much do you need?
Retail investors bid up to two lakh for a thirty-five percent quota,
with allotment by lottery if oversubscribed.
H-N-Is go above two lakh for a fifteen percent quota.
For Molbio, one lot is eighteen shares —
about fourteen thousand five hundred and twenty-six rupees —
your minimum.
Track the live subscription on the N-S-E and B-S-E I-P-O pages,
Chittorgarh, Moneycontrol, or your broker app.
Let's recap Molbio Diagnostics.
A unique,
made-in-India point-of-care testing company behind the Truenat platform,
fast-growing and profitable,
with revenue up over forty percent.
But nearly eighty percent of the issue is a sell-down,
and it has no listed peer —
so there's no P-E to tell you if the price is fair.
The retail minimum is about fourteen thousand five hundred and twenty-six rupees,
and the grey-market premium is near twenty-two percent,
though unofficial.
This video explains the IPO for education only —
it is not investment advice,
not a buy or sell recommendation,
and not a prediction of listing gains.
Grey-market premium is unofficial and changes hourly.
Always read the RHP and check the live subscription before you apply.
Thanks for watching.
